name: pratt-parser
intent: Parse expressions with many prefix, infix and postfix operators by associating a binding power and a handler with each token type, so precedence and associativity live in one rule table instead of one parsing function per precedence level.
problem: Operator precedence turns expression parsing into a ladder of near-identical functions - one per level - each of which must re-implement associativity, delegate to the next level for its operands, and be edited whenever an operator is added or moves. Grammars with prefix, infix, postfix and mixfix operators (ternary conditionals, assignment, calls, indexing, user-registered operators) make that ladder long, make associativity easy to get subtly wrong, and scatter the grammar across the parser so it cannot be read in one place.
context: Hand-written parsers for an expression-bearing language, DSL, query or configuration syntax: a token stream is already available (or is cheap to lex), the operator set is large or expected to grow, and the team wants the grammar visible as data. It is typically the expression layer under an ordinary recursive-descent parser for statements and declarations - interpreters, calculators, filter and rule engines, formula tools - and it is unnecessary when a parser generator already declares precedence for the grammar.
benefits: Precedence and associativity become data: adding an operator is one rule row (token, handlers, binding power), not a new function plus a new call site in every level above it.
A single expression loop replaces the per-level ladder, so grammar changes no longer ripple through the parser and cannot leave a level out of sync.

Prefix, infix, postfix and mixfix operators all fit the same two hooks - a null-denotation handler that starts an expression and a left-denotation handler that extends one - including tokens that are both (minus, star, left parenthesis).

Associativity is expressed mechanically: recurse with the operator's own binding power for right-associative operators and with one more for left-associative ones, instead of hand-coding each level's grouping.
Single pass, left to right, no backtracking: work is linear in tokens, and positions, errors and recovery attach to a small number of functions.
The grammar is reviewable and extensible in one place, which is also the registration point for plugin- or user-defined operators.
tradeoffs: The table is indirection: a wrong binding power or associativity produces a silently different tree, not a compile-time or parse error, and only tests over operator combinations catch it.
Recursion is proportional to operator nesting and to the length of left-associative chains, so hostile or generated input can exhaust the call stack unless a nesting-depth guard is added.

A token often needs two rules (prefix and infix) and table completeness becomes part of the grammar; a missing or empty row surfaces as a crash or a generic "unexpected token" instead of a grammar diagnostic.
Error messages and recovery are hand-crafted per handler; a parser generator's generated diagnostics are usually better for free.
The loop is small but intertwined - binding powers, lookahead and handler dispatch must all be right at once - so the pattern reads as simple only after it is understood.

Grammar-as-data is harder to review than a BNF-like grammar: a reviewer must reconstruct precedence from table order and constants, and nothing in the source states the precedence hierarchy explicitly.

participants.responsibility: Consumes a token, dispatches it to its prefix handler, then repeatedly extends the resulting expression through left handlers while the lookahead token binds at least as tightly as the caller's minimum binding power.

Parses constructs that start an expression - literals, names, grouping, prefix operators - recursing through the loop with the binding power that decides how much of the following input belongs to the operand.

Parses constructs that extend an already parsed expression - binary operators, calls, indexing, ternary conditionals, postfix operators - receiving the left operand and choosing its right operand's binding power.
Maps each token type to its handlers and its binding power: the grammar in data form and the extension point for new operators.

Numeric precedence of a token as an infix or postfix operator; comparison against the caller's minimum decides whether the loop stops, and associativity is derived by recursing with the power itself or with one more.
Produces the typed tokens with source positions the loop consumes; deliberately kept separate and simpler than the parser.

use_cases: Expression evaluators and calculators whose operator set is expected to grow (arithmetic, units, comparisons, percentages, function calls, user-defined functions).
Query, filter and rule languages - search filters, feature-flag conditions, access-policy conditions, spreadsheet formulas - with many comparison, logical and string operators.
Front ends for small languages and DSLs that parse statements and declarations with recursive descent and need real precedence handling for the expression layer.
Single-pass compilers and interpreters that emit bytecode or IR while parsing, where each handler is also the point that emits the operator's instruction.
Template and configuration expression languages that must attach exact source positions and precise errors to every operator.
Host-language extension points that let plugins or users register additional operators at runtime, because registration is just a table entry.
Rust PEG grammars that use pest::pratt_parser::PrattParser to map prefix, postfix and infix operator pairs into calculator or DSL ASTs.
Rust parser-combinator expression grammars built with chumsky's pratt combinator, where atom parsers and prefix, postfix and infix operators declare precedence and associativity.
JavaScript expression-only tooling built on JSEP, where a compact Pratt-style parser produces ASTs and allows custom unary and binary operators with explicit precedence.
avoid_when: The grammar is mostly statements and declarations with only two or three operator levels: plain recursive descent is shorter and clearer.
A parser generator already fits the workflow (yacc/bison, ANTLR, lark, pest, pegen): declaring precedence in the grammar beats hand-maintaining a table.
The expression language is small, fixed and fully determined by a data format: a shunting-yard pass or a table-driven evaluator is enough.
You need incremental, error-tolerant or IDE-grade re-parsing (editors, language servers): use a parser framework built for that instead of a hand-rolled loop.

A maintained parser and syntax tree for the target syntax already exists (Roslyn for C#, go/parser for Go, the TypeScript compiler API, SwiftParser/SwiftSyntax): write a Pratt parser only for a grammar of your own.
anti_patterns: One function per precedence level with a comment calling it a Pratt parser: the table and binding powers were never introduced, so the pattern's benefit is absent.
Precedence written as an if/else chain over operator spellings inside the loop, so operator extensions touch the core algorithm and the grammar is no longer data.
Binding powers without associativity - recursing with the operator's own power for left-associative operators - which turns a - b - c into a - (b - c).
Growing the loop into a general grammar engine (statements, declarations, scopes, all in one table) instead of leaving Pratt parsing to the expression layer.
Running a hand-written parser over untrusted expressions with no nesting limit, accepting stack exhaustion as the error path.
design_principles: Data over control flow: token behaviour and binding power live in a table, so the grammar is inspectable and extensible.
Separation of concerns: lexing, dispatch, precedence resolution and semantic action are distinct, each with one job.
Open/closed: new operators are added by registering handlers, without modifying the parsing loop.
Uniformity: prefix, infix, postfix and mixfix operators share two handler shapes, removing the special case per arity.
Explicit precedence and associativity: both are named numeric properties of a token rather than an accident of the call structure.
best_practices: Give every token type a row even when it is empty, and decide prefix vs infix explicitly: tokens such as minus or left parenthesis legitimately need both handlers.

Choose the recursion power mechanically - lbp + 1 for left-associative operators, lbp for right-associative ones, a power above the operand level for prefix operators - and document the convention next to the table.
Guard recursion with an explicit depth limit that raises a positioned parse error before the host language's stack limit is reached.

Keep the grammar in one place (a readable table or a single registration function) and test it with a golden-tree matrix over operator pairs, covering every precedence boundary and both associativities.
Report errors at the offending token with the expected set; the loop knows the minimum binding power, so "unexpected operator here" is cheap and precise.
Keep parseExpression(minBp) reusable and the handlers free of statement-level parsing, so the expression layer can be lifted into another grammar.
sources: Pratt, V. R. (1973). Top Down Operator Precedence. Proceedings of the 1st annual ACM SIGACT-SIGPLAN Symposium on Principles of Programming Languages (POPL '73), Boston - the originating paper: tokens carry a null denotation, a left denotation and a binding power, and one loop resolves precedence.
